::: {.cite-bar .domain-foundations}
[Superseded]{.status .status-superseded} [Pub. L. 64-85]{.cite} [39 Stat. 166]{.cite} [10 U.S.C. 10101 et seq.]{.cite}
:::

The first comprehensive statute organizing U.S. land forces. It defined the Army as the Regular Army, the National Guard, and a federal reserve, and it let the President draft the Guard into federal service for use overseas.

## Key provisions

- Defined the components of the Army and expanded its authorized strength.
- Guard members took a dual oath to state and nation and could be drafted into federal service in war.
- Created the Reserve Officers' Training Corps and an organized reserve.
- Gave the President authority to place obligatory orders with industry in war, an early precedent for defense production powers.

## Why it matters

It set the three-component structure the Army still has. The 1933 amendments completed the design by making Guard members simultaneously members of a federal reserve component, which is what today's [mobilization authorities](reserve-mobilization.qmd) operate on. Its industrial mobilization section anticipates the [Defense Production Act](dpa-1950.qmd).

## Current status

Amended heavily in 1920 and 1933 and absorbed into Titles 10 and 32 by the 1956 codification.
